result.summary: Telemachus and Pisistratus are welcomed at Menelaus' palace in Lacedaemon, where Helen and Menelaus recognise Telemachus. Menelaus tells how Proteus revealed the fates of Ajax, Agamemnon and Ulysses. Back in Ithaca the suitors plot an ambush, Penelope despairs, and Minerva comforts her with a dream.

scenes.title: Arrival at Menelaus' wedding feast
scenes.summary: Telemachus and Pisistratus are received and fed in Menelaus' splendid house during his children's wedding feast.

scenes.title: Helen, Menelaus and grief for Ulysses
scenes.summary: Menelaus laments his losses and Ulysses' absence; Helen recognises Telemachus, drugs the wine, and both tell tales of Ulysses at Troy.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus seeks news of his father amid grief.

scenes.title: Telemachus asks about his father
scenes.summary: At dawn Telemachus explains his errand and the suitors' abuse; Menelaus is outraged.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus' estate and household are being consumed by the suitors.

scenes.title: Menelaus and Proteus on Pharos
scenes.summary: Becalmed on Pharos, Menelaus is helped by Idothea to seize Proteus, who reveals the deaths of Ajax and Agamemnon and that Ulysses is held by Calypso.
scenes.stakes: Menelaus and his men risk starvation and being unable to get home.

scenes.title: Gifts offered to Telemachus
scenes.summary: Menelaus offers horses; Telemachus declines and accepts a silver mixing bowl instead.

scenes.title: The suitors plan an ambush
scenes.summary: Noemon reveals Telemachus has gone to Pylos; Antinous resolves to ambush him.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus' life is threatened by the suitors.

scenes.title: Penelope's grief and Minerva's dream
scenes.summary: Medon tells Penelope of the plot; Euryclea confesses and urges prayer, and Minerva sends a comforting vision.
scenes.stakes: Penelope fears losing her son as well as her husband.

scenes.title: Ambush at Asteris
scenes.summary: The suitors sail and lie in wait at the islet of Asteris.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus will be ambushed on his return.

Helen's care-banishing drug, often compared to nepenthe.

analysis.text: Grief, memory and hospitality run through the book; the tales of Agamemnon's murder warn of a bad homecoming and contrast with Ulysses' hoped-for return.
The lavish gifts, guest-friendship rituals and travelling for news reflect the Homeric code of xenia.

legacy.text: Proteus gave English the adjective protean, meaning changeable.
Helen's drug gave rise to the term nepenthe in later literature.

fun_facts.text: Menelaus' list of travels, including Libya's horned lambs, shows early Greek knowledge of distant lands.

language_notes.text: Menelaus is marrying his daughter Hermione to Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, a match promised during the Trojan War. The bracketed number 36 is a footnote marker.
Myrmidons were Achilles' people, from Phthia in Thessaly. Neoptolemus now rules them.
Vouchsafed means graciously granted; here heaven granted Helen no more children after Hermione.
Tumblers were acrobats who performed in the middle of the hall while the bard played.
Anointing with oil after bathing was normal hospitality, leaving guests fresh and clothed in clean garments.
A ewer is a jug for pouring water; the maid pours it over their hands into the basin.
"Fall to" means begin eating. Hosts traditionally fed guests before asking their names.
Loin is a prime cut of meat, given to guests as a mark of honour.
Menelaus lists lands he wandered through after Troy; the Erembians are an obscure people, and Libya's horned lambs and thrice-yearly lambing are traveller's marvels.
Menelaus's brother Agamemnon was murdered on his return by Aegisthus and Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra while Menelaus was away.
Perfidy means treachery, a betrayal of trust.
Diana is the Roman name for the huntress goddess (Greek Artemis), used here as a standard of beauty.
A talent was a measure of weight in precious metal; a tripod was a three-legged cauldron or stand, valued as a gift.
A distaff is a staff that holds raw wool or flax for spinning into yarn.
Helen refers to her elopement with Paris, which caused the Trojan War; she calls herself shameless.
Antilochus, Nestor's son, was killed at Troy by Memnon, the son of Dawn (Eos), an Ethiopian king.
Cutting the hair and weeping were customary mourning rites for the dead; here the speaker (Pisistratus) says these are the only honours the living can give.
The drug is often identified with nepenthe, the 'sorrow-banishing' drug in Homer's Greek; the translation gives only 'an herb'.
Paeeon was the physician of the gods in Greek tradition, so Egyptians are called his race, meaning they are skilled healers.
'A tale in season' means a story suited to the occasion; Helen offers talk to replace tears.
The wooden horse was the trick by which Greek warriors hid inside and entered Troy. Deiphobus was a Trojan prince who married Helen after Paris died.
Helen is said to have imitated the voices of the warriors' wives to tempt the hidden men into revealing themselves.
Homeric formula for daybreak, repeated throughout the poem; 'child of morning' and 'rosy-fingered' are fixed descriptions of Dawn.
'Eaten out of house and home' means the suitors are consuming his household's wealth and food supplies.
'Miscreants' means villains or wrongdoers; here it refers to the suitors.
'Suppliant' means one who humbly begs for help; 'haply' is an archaic word for 'perhaps'.
'Usurp a brave man's bed' means to take the place of the husband as Penelope's mate and master of the house.
'Short shrift' means little time or mercy before punishment; the 'sorry wedding' is a grim joke about their courtship.
'Prevaricate' means to avoid the truth by evasive talk.
The 'old man of the sea' is Proteus, the sea god who told Menelaus news of Ulysses; Menelaus caught him while he changed shape.
A hecatomb was originally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen; here it means any large sacrificial offering. 'Dues' are the honours the gods expect.
'In the person of Idothea' means through the agency of Idothea, a goddess acting as his rescuer.
'Head man' is a colloquial rendering: Proteus is Neptune's chief servant, tending his seals.
'Furs the water' means the West wind ruffles the surface into a rough, dark texture.
Halosydne ('sea-nurtured') is a title of Amphitrite, Neptune's wife, so seals are called her 'chickens', her flock.
'Child of morning rosy-fingered Dawn' is Homer's stock formula for daybreak.
Ambrosia is the fragrant food of the gods, here used as a divine perfume against the stench.
'Son of Atreus' names Menelaus by his father; Proteus recognises him before being told.
A hecatomb was originally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen; in Homer it means any large, solemn sacrifice to the gods.
"Heaven-fed" translates a Homeric epithet for the Nile, meaning swollen by rain from the sky; the river is called by a stock phrase.
Ajax here is the lesser Ajax, son of Oileus, who offended Minerva at Troy by dragging Cassandra from her altar. He is not the Telamonian Ajax.
Malea is the stormy southeastern cape of the Peloponnese, notorious for blowing ships off course.
Thyestes was Agamemnon's uncle and Aegisthus's father; his feud with Atreus' family explains why Aegisthus lived there and hated Agamemnon.
"Cloister" here means the colonnaded hall or courtyard of the palace, not a monastery.
Orestes, Agamemnon's son, avenged his father by killing Aegisthus. Proteus hints that the funeral feast may already be happening.
Elysium (the Elysian plain) is a blessed land at the world's edge where favoured heroes live after death, without dying in the usual way.
A chalice here is a cup or goblet; a drink-offering (libation) was wine poured out to the gods before or during a meal.
"A piece of plate" means an object of precious metal, such as a silver or gold vessel, not a dish for food.
Lotus here is a clover-like fodder plant good for horses, not the narcotic lotus of the Lotus-eaters.
Meadow-sweet is a fragrant flowering meadow plant; here it is named as part of the rich pasture of Menelaus's plains.
A mixing bowl (crater) was a large vessel in which wine was blended with water before serving.
Menelaus stopped in Phoenicia (Sidon) on his long, wandering return from Troy, which he describes earlier in Book 4.
The square brackets mark lines the translator treats as doubtful or as an editorial addition, so they may not belong to the original.
"Discs" are heavy throwing stones or plates, used in athletic contests like the modern discus.
"Brood mares" are mares kept for breeding; "not yet broken in" means the unbroken mule foals have never been trained to work.
"City of Neleus" is Pylos, ruled by Nestor, son of Neleus. Telemachus has gone there to seek news of his father.
"Bondsmen" are slaves or servants bound to a master, as opposed to free men.
Mentor is Ulysses' old friend; the goddess Minerva has taken his shape to accompany Telemachus, hence "some god".
Samos here is the island also called Same (Cephallenia), west of Ithaca. The narrow strait between is a natural place for an ambush.
"Sea-horses" is a poetic image for ships, which carry men over the water as horses carry them over land.
"Hellas and middle Argos" means Greece at large and the Argive region; it is a way of saying Ulysses' fame reached everywhere.
Bruised barley means crushed barley grains, offered with prayer as a sacrificial gift.
Burning fat thigh bones was the standard sacrifice to gods. Penelope appeals to Ulysses' past offerings as a debt Minerva should repay.
Thole-pins are pegs set in the ship's side that hold the oars in place while rowing.
The thong-hole is the hole in the door through which a leather strap passed to pull the door shut. The vision enters like a draught.
Hades is the god of the dead and the name of his underworld realm; "the house of Hades" means death.
Asteris lies in the strait between Ithaca and Samos, which makes it a good spot to intercept ships returning to Ithaca.

context_notes.text: Helen, Menelaus' wife, was the cause of the Trojan War after Paris took her to Troy. Venus is the Greek Aphrodite.
Menelaus spent years wandering before returning from Troy, so he knows the need for hospitality to travellers.
Jove's Olympian palace was imagined as the most dazzling of dwellings, so Telemachus' comparison shows how rich Sparta seems.
Menelaus, king of Sparta and Helen's husband, is entertaining Telemachus and Pisistratus, who have come seeking news of Ulysses.
Helen's attendants and her costly Egyptian gifts reflect Menelaus's wealth and his long stay in Egypt on the journey home.
Nestor, king of Pylos, was an old and wise Achaean leader, so Telemachus visited him first for news of his father.
Antilochus, Nestor's son, was killed at Troy. Telemachus has just heard of him through Nestor's household, so Pisistratus speaks of him here.
Helen is called Jove's daughter because, in tradition, Zeus (Jove) was her father.
Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) helped Paris take Helen to Troy, which caused the Trojan War. Helen here blames the goddess.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is said to have led Helen away from the horse, saving the hidden Greeks.
Lacedaemon is the region of Sparta, ruled by Menelaus, husband of Helen.
Telemachus asks as a suppliant, invoking the sacred duty of hospitality owed to guests and those seeking help.
Jove (the Greek Zeus), Minerva (Athena) and Apollo are gods Menelaus swears by; this oath wishes Ulysses's old strength back.
Pharos was an island off the Nile delta, later the site of Alexandria's famous lighthouse.
Proteus is a sea god who tends Neptune's seals, knows all things, and can change shape.
Counting on his fingers shows Proteus as a shepherd of the sea, with seals as his flock.
Menelaus is addressed as son of Atreus, his father. He is king of Sparta and brother of Agamemnon.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea and earthquakes; his weapon is the trident.
Menelaus's marriage to Helen, daughter of Jove (the Greek Zeus), makes him the god's son-in-law and earns him this special afterlife.
A barrow is a burial mound; Menelaus raises an empty tomb for Agamemnon to honour him, since the body lay at Mycenae.
Pylos is the home of Nestor, where Telemachus left his ship and crew before travelling overland to Sparta.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) was the divine smith, so an object made by him is a marvel of craftsmanship.
Antinous and Eurymachus are the most prominent suitors, competing for Penelope's hand while consuming Ulysses' household goods.
Jove, king of the gods (the Greek Zeus), is invoked here as a power that can end a life.
Dolius is a household servant given to Penelope at her marriage. Laertes is Ulysses' aged father, who lives apart in the countryside.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Jove's daughter and protects Ulysses' family. Aegis-bearing refers to Jove's goatskin shield, the aegis.
The vision takes the form of Penelope's sister so that Penelope will trust it. Gods in Homer often send dreams in the shape of a loved one.

literary_notes.text: Menelaus' rebuke of Eteoneus shows him as generous, mindful of hospitality and aware of his own past hardships.
The house's splendour is compared to the sun and moon, conveying radiance and wonder through a bright, cosmic image.
Comparing Menelaus' hall to Jove's palace exaggerates its glory to express Telemachus' awe.
The pithy saying that crying is cold comfort gives Menelaus's grief a practical, worldly tone.
Menelaus mourns Ulysses before his hearer, unaware that the silent young man is Ulysses' son.
Comparing Helen to Diana shows her striking beauty and her near-divine presence as she enters.
Helen's self-blame shows her as perceptive and still burdened by guilt for the war.
The extreme examples of parents dying and a son hewn to pieces stress the drug's power over grief.
Helen shows Ulysses as so cunning that even she cannot get information from him, and shows herself as sharp-eyed.
Telemachus mourns his father's courage as useless, while the audience knows Ulysses is still alive and may yet return.
Menelaus is compared to an immortal god, stressing his dignity and royal splendor as Telemachus's host.
Telemachus's complaint portrays him as dutiful but powerless, a young man oppressed in his own home.
The hind and lion image shows the suitors as timid intruders and Ulysses as the lion whose return will bring violent retribution.
The wrestling match recalls Ulysses's past strength, lifting hope that he may still be alive and able to avenge his house.
Proteus counting his seals is compared to a shepherd among sheep, giving the sea god a familiar pastoral image.
Idothea's list of transformations prepares the later struggle, so the reader knows what to expect.
The rhetorical question about sleeping with a sea monster adds a wry, personal aside to the narrator's account.
The rapid list of forms, lion, dragon, leopard, boar, water, tree, conveys Proteus's shifting and the men's steady grip.
Ajax's boast that even the gods cannot drown him brings his destruction, a typical Homeric lesson against defying the gods.
"Drank salt water" gives Ajax's drowning a grimly understated, almost ironic turn after his boast.
Comparing Agamemnon's killing to butchering an ox makes the murder brutal and shows the betrayal of a banquet host.
Menelaus's feeling that he cannot bear to see sunlight expresses the depth of his grief.
Telemachus shows courtesy and tact, praising his host's talk while firmly putting his mission first, which marks his growing maturity.
Telemachus sets Sparta's broad plains against rocky Ithaca, turning a polite refusal into affectionate pride in his homeland.
The divinely made silver bowl stands for the honor and guest-friendship between the two houses.
The suitors' idle games and "old insolence" show them carefree and arrogant, setting up the shock of Telemachus's departure.
The reader knows Minerva was in Mentor's form, so Noemon's puzzlement is explained to us but not to him.
A "black" heart and eyes that "flashed fire" vividly convey Antinous's fury through darkness and flame.
Antinous's plan to ambush Telemachus in the straits sets up a danger that will threaten the rest of the story.
The suitors mock the queen's ignorance while the audience knows she has just learned of the plot and prayed to Minerva.
The narrator hints that the suitors' confidence is misplaced and that events will turn against them.
Penelope is compared to a lioness hemmed in by hunters, showing her fear and helplessness.
The vision's curt refusal keeps the divine messenger's limits clear and leaves Penelope's uncertainty about Ulysses unresolved.
